headline: From frightened fawn in ‘Bambi’ to decorated Marine and Vietnam vet
author: Amanda Covarrubias

paragraphs.text: Millions of moviegoers knew his voice, if not his name.

Donnie Dunagan gave auditory life to the frightened fawn in Disney’s 1942 animated classic “Bambi,” creating an indelible mark on the minds of moviegoers in the harrowing scene where young Bambi calls for his mother after hunters shoot and kill her.

The movie would be his last. Mr. Dunagan went on to join the Marine Corps at age 18. He served for 25 years and became a decorated veteran, earning three Purple Hearts, among many other medals, and retired as a major.

During most of his time in the Marines, Mr. Dunagan kept his Hollywood past a secret from those who served with him. He didn’t want them confusing their commanding officer with Bambi, and he didn’t want to boast.

“I am a commander in Marine Corps boot camp,” Mr. Dunagan told StoryCorps in 2015. “Hundreds of recruits I’m responsible for. ... I just thought to myself, I don’t think I want all these young Marines to start calling me ‘Major Bambi,’ and I kept my mouth shut.”

He told the Guardian in 2005: “You have to understand what it’s like in the Marine Corps, or in the CIA, or FBI. Those were the best men I ever met in my life, but they would never talk about their past, or boast about their achievements. Because only tacky men did that.”
Mr. Dunagan died Nov. 4 at 92, in San Angelo, Texas, his representatives said. They did not provide a cause of death, but he had suffered from lung cancer.
He came to play the voice of young Bambi in Disney’s 1942 animated classic after being scouted by a talent agent when he was 3 years old.
He appeared in several movies before “Bambi,” including as Peter von Frankenstein, the grandson of the mad scientist, in “Son of Frankenstein” in 1939.
But “Bambi” would turn out to be his last movie role. A decade after it premiered, during the Korean War, he joined the Marines.

He served three tours in Vietnam and trained recruits for combat as the Corps’ youngest drill instructor, according to an Air Force website. He also served as a counterintelligence officer before retiring in 1977.
Donald Roan Dunagan was born Aug. 16, 1934, in San Antonio. During the Depression, his family moved to Memphis, where they lived in a two-room flat.

On a corner down the street, a man would dance “like you would not believe,” he told USA Today. One day his mother took him there, and Donnie started imitating him. They became a duet and soon after performed in a big talent show in Memphis.
“I won the darn thing,” he said. “Someone in the audience got in touch with my parents asking if I could go to Hollywood to audition for a couple roles — they needed a runt kid like me.”
In addition to voicing young Bambi, Mr. Dunagan served as the character’s real-life model for the animators, spending months in front of illustrators, following their commands.

“Look left, look right, look afraid. When Bambi is kissed by a doe, he gives a look of disgust. We spent an hour on that look.” he said. “‘Look like something bad has happened,’ they’d say. But I was having the time of my life. Finally someone said, ‘Pretend like you just had castor oil.’ That did it.”

He called Walt Disney “a wonderful guy” who took him to a meeting in Los Angeles where Disney offered the image of Bambi to the forestry department to use in a campaign to raise awareness about forest fires.
“Look at this face,” Disney said at the meeting, according to Mr. Dunagan. “This is the face of Bambi.”
Mr. Dunagan ended up making seven movies in all, and became his family’s breadwinner. But Hollywood took a toll.

“It turned out that all that money hurt my family,” he told the Guardian. “We’d gone from a one-room tenement to a house in Beverly Hills, and it was too much, too quick. The family just ruptured, and I was then farmed out to a bunch of people.”
After his parents divorced, Dunagan spent time in several boarding homes, played football and boxed in high school, and supported himself before joining the military.

His efforts to hide his “Bambi” past worked until he was near retirement, the same year the animated film was rereleased in theaters. One day his commanding general called him into his office and told him he wanted Mr. Dunagan to audit some auditors on base.

The commanding general pulled down his glasses and patted a red folder on his desk “from an old security clearance I had from years ago,” Mr. Dunagan told USA Today. He began to protest that he was too busy, but the commanding general would have none of it.
“You will audit the auditors,” the commanding general said. “Won’t you … Major Bambi?”
As Mr. Dunagan grew older, he would come to soften his stance toward his most famous Hollywood role. He attended screenings and fan events, while continuing to encourage and support other veterans.
He participated in a DVD release of “Bambi” and spoke at conventions and festivals as an ambassador for the film for many years.
He is survived by his wife of 34 years, Dana Dunagan.
Mr. Dunagan said there were few accomplishments he could have achieved that would have overshadowed his role in “Bambi.”

“I have some holes in my body that God didn’t put there,” Dunagan said in the StoryCorps interview. “I got shot through my left knee. Got an award or two for saving lives over time, but I think I could have been appointed as the aide de camp in the White House. It wouldn’t make any difference.
“It’s Bambi that’s so dear to people, but I love it now when people realize this old jerk is still alive and was Bambi, and I wouldn’t take anything for it, not a darn thing for it.”
